chapterOverview.guidingQuestion: What are the characteristic properties and behaviors of waves?
chapterOverview.purpose: The purpose of this component idea is to understand the properties of waves -- both pulses and simple waves -- as well as the behaviors that we observe when waves interact with each other or their surroundings.
chapterOverview.centralIdeas: Waves transfer energy without permanently displacing matter. A wave pulse forms when a push or pull transfers energy to a medium that a wave can travel through. Many things can produce energy pulses -- objects striking a surface, vibrations of vocal cords, shifting of tectonic plates, the rearrangement of subatomic particles, etc. Repetitive pulses produce a simple wave pattern with certain properties. The wavelength, and therefore speed, of a wave is influenced by properties of the medium that transmits the wave.

K-2.nrcQuote: By the end of grade 2. Waves, which are regular patterns of motion, can be made in water by disturbing the surface. When waves move across the surface of deep water, the water goes up and down in place; it does not move in the direction of the wave---observe, for example, a bobbing cork or seabird---except when the water meets the beach. Sound can make matter vibrate, and vibrating matter can make sound. -- NRC, 2012
K-2.progression:
Young children often observe sound and water waves in daily life---splashing in a tub or pool, tossing rocks into a pond, or hearing music, voices and sudden sounds. These experiences form the foundation for learning about waves.

At this stage, students aren't expected to understand energy or energy transfer, but they do learn that motion in one place can cause motion elsewhere. If students repeat a splash (like three quick taps on the water surface), they can observe the waves radiate outwards and notice the object bobs three times. This shows that waves carry patterns of motion across the water.

These water wave observations also support early ideas about sound. While students don't yet understand that air is a medium, they can begin linking sound to vibration---like noticing that a tuning fork stops sounding when it stops vibrating, or that clapping causes rice on paper to jump.

3-5.nrcQuote:
By the end of grade 5. Waves of the same type can differ in amplitude (height of the wave) and wavelength (spacing between wave peaks). Waves can add or cancel one another as they cross, depending on their relative phase (i.e., relative position of peaks and troughs of the waves), but they emerge unaffected by each other. (Boundary: The discussion at this grade level is qualitative only; it can be based on the fact that two different sounds can pass a location in different directions without getting mixed up.)

Earthquakes cause seismic waves, which are waves of motion in Earth's crust. -- NRC, 2012
3-5.progression:
Learning that matter exists in invisible forms is a key physical science development that unlocks many late elementary grades concepts, including that air is not empty space. Air is a medium that can transmit motion with behaviors that match the behaviors of water in earlier grades.

Students should have multiple experiences observing various properties of waves. For example, waves can have different heights depending on the amount of energy that went into the production of the wave. Waves produced by a steady source produce a sequence of waves with consistent spacing.

Students should begin to explore behaviors of waves that occur when waves interact with each other. Late elementary standards focus on interactions that happen as waves interact with each other. The behaviors are easiest to see using systems where individual wave pulses can be isolated.

As students learn that Earth has an internal structure, they are prepared to fuse those ideas with ideas about seismic waves.

6-8.nrcQuote:
By the end of grade 8. A simple wave has a repeating pattern with a specific wavelength, frequency, and amplitude. A sound wave needs a medium through which it is transmitted.

Geologists use seismic waves and their reflection at interfaces between layers to probe structures deep in the planet. -- NRC, 2012
6-8.progression:
Throughout elementary school, students may have explored waves by creating ripples in shallow pans of water. They learned that wave height and spacing depend on how a disturbance is made and that waves transfer energy from one place to another without moving the medium itself.

In middle school, students build on these ideas by recognizing that a repeating disturbance creates a simple wave. A simple wave is one with a regular pattern where the frequency matches the number of vibrations or pulses per second from the source. Students can now use this understanding to model sound as a wave---specifically, a pressure wave made of compressions and rarefactions caused by vibrating objects like tuning forks, speakers, or vocal cords. This helps explain why sound requires a medium and cannot travel through empty space.

Seismic waves are introduced in this grade band to show how wave properties apply to real-world phenomena. Disturbances within Earth's crust generate multiple types of waves that travel through Earth's interior.

table.waveProperties: Waves are caused by disturbances and travel away from the disturbance that causes them.
table.waveBehaviors: Waves cause objects to bob up and down without traveling with the wave. Vibrating materials make sound and sound, in turn, can make things move.

table.waveProperties: Features of disturbances influence the amplitude of a wave pulse and spacing between pulses.
table.waveBehaviors: Waves of the same type interact at the point where they cross paths but continue unaffected afterward.

table.waveProperties: Simple wave patterns are caused by repetitive disturbances.
table.waveBehaviors: Waves transmit energy through matter (e.g., water waves, sound waves, waves on a stretched spring).

table.waveProperties: Wave speed is determined by characteristics of the medium.
table.waveBehaviors: Waves reflect, refract, and transmit in different ways when crossing from one medium to another. Materials can be caused to vibrate by certain wave frequencies.

progression.narrative: This progression can unfold through repeated investigations using a consistent set of materials---such as a shallow pan of water and one or more tuning forks. In the earliest grades, students observe how a disturbance to the water's surface creates ripples that move outward. In late elementary, using two tuning forks at once lets students observe how wave patterns can interact as they pass through each other without changing which helps explain that distinct voices can be heard - even in noisy environments. These experiences help students in middle school visualize simple waves, including sound. By high school, the same materials support investigations into how the medium affects wave speed and behaviors like reflection, refraction, and resonance.

standards.statement: Plan and conduct investigations to demonstrate the cause-and-effect relationship between vibrating materials and sound.
standards.bigIdea: Vibrating materials (motion) can cause sound, and sound can cause vibrations (motion) in objects. (Note: Some sounds originate because of moving air and it may be difficult for students to identify air as the source of the vibration. Examples should focus on objects that produce a sound such as clapping hands, leaves rustling in trees, striking of a hammer, plucking a guitar string.)
scientificIdeas: Striking an object can cause it to vibrate. When it vibrates, it moves back and forth repeatedly.
Vibrations can be fast or slow, and they can last for different amounts of time (e.g., a single clap vs. humming).
Some vibrating materials produce sounds we can hear.
When a vibrating object stops moving or is prevented from vibrating, it stops making sound.
Sounds can cause objects to vibrate---for example, grains of rice on a drumhead will bounce when sound reaches them.
Hitting an object harder makes it louder; softer makes it quieter.
A tuning fork placed in water shows visible ripples moving outward which travel towards other objects on the water's surface, helping students link sound at one place to motion at a distant place.
studentIdeas: Some sounds exist without being caused by a vibration (e.g., snapping fingers, crickets, television).
Only musical instruments make sound.
Sound can only move in straight lines and not around obstacles that block its path or around corners.
When we cover our mouths, sound gets trapped so we cannot hear it.
Vibrations only happen when something is hit hard.
Quiet sounds don't cause any vibration at all.
Vibrations can only happen in solids, not in air or water.
If you can't see or feel something move, it's not vibrating.

standards.statement: Use a model of a simple wave to describe amplitude, wavelength, and explain how waves can add or cancel each other as they cross.
standards.bigIdea: Waves have measurable properties that vary and depend on the actions that caused the wave to form. It is possible to create a representation of a wave's properties.
scientificIdeas: A wave forms when a force (push or pull) disturbs a medium, causing it to move. A single disturbance creates a wave pulse. Repeated disturbances create a simple wave.
Disturbances caused by stronger forces create more motion in the medium (e.g., water, stretched spring) and therefore taller waves.
Stronger forces push or pull harder on the medium (e.g., water, rope, stretched spring), producing taller waves.
The distance between wave pulses depends on the timing between disturbances; more time between pulses leads to greater spacing.
Waves transfer energy away from the point of disturbance.
Although waves move through a medium, the particles in the medium return to their original positions once the wave has passed---they are not carried with the wave.
When waves are in the same place at the same time, they can add together or cancel each other out.
Waves at the same place and time completely cancel each other out if their phases are opposite -- when a crest and valley of equal energy meet.
Crests and troughs will only partially cancel each other when they intersect if they were produced by forces of different strengths.
When a pair of wave crests or wave troughs intersect, their energies combine for a moment to create greater disturbance.
Simple waves can pass through each other without permanent change after they pass.
studentIdeas: Waves are objects that collide and bounce off each other.
Bigger waves destroy or cancel smaller waves when they collide.
Waves only happen on water.
If two waves meet, they will stop or block each other.
Waves always add together to make a bigger wave.
The effects of waves interfering with each other are permanent.

standards.statement: Develop and use models to represent the basic properties of waves in a system including frequency, amplitude, wavelength, and speed.
standards.bigIdea: Wave properties describe the repeating patterns of waves formed by disturbances.
scientificIdeas: A simple wave is formed by repeated disturbances to a medium.
The waves travel and transfer energy away from the source of the disturbance.
Stronger forces produce waves that displace greater amounts of the medium.
Disturbances that occur more frequently produce waves that are closer together.
Media allow waves to travel at different speeds. Wavelengths will be longer in media where waves travel faster because each wave pulse travels further before the next forms.
Sound waves are simple waves caused by vibrating materials, such as tuning forks, speakers, vocal cords, etc.
Models of sound waves represent the high (peaks) and low (valleys) pressure bands produced as the source vibrates.
studentIdeas: Waves slow down as they move through a medium, just like objects do.
Frequency and speed are the same thing.
All waves move at the same speed regardless of the medium.
Wave properties are unrelated to how the wave was created or what it moves through.
The frequency of a disturbance can change without affecting the wavelength of the resulting wave.
Some waves form without an input of energy.
